newsitem.title: KENYA: Military option in Zaire wanes.
newsitem.headline: Military option in Zaire wanes.

text.p: Momentum for a foreign military force in eastern Zaire was waning on Monday as a civilian relief operation for millions of needy people took shape.
The United States and Britain backed further away from the French-backed military option, citing its imprecise goals.
Africa's number one military power, South Africa, is refusing to be pressured into action.
Ethiopia was one of Africa's two candidates to join a multinational force but complained on Monday about having to pay for its own contingent.

"You can't go rushing in with troops without knowing what the mission is, the scope of responsibility and who's going to pay for it," said U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns, summing up the sceptics' view.
The military option is fraught with risks and its sponsors have failed to answer basic questions.
"No-one knows the exact situation on the ground, no-one knows what the intervention force would do -- intervene between whom and whom?" asked a senior diplomat in the region.

Rwanda and the rebels now controlling much of eastern Zaire firmly oppose any role in a military force for France -- the leading volunteer. African leaders implicitly backed this stand by calling last week for a "neutral force".
The Tutsis in charge in Rwanda and those among the rebels oppose France for two reasons:
-- it backed the former Hutu regime in Rwanda which committed the 1994 genocide against minority Tutsis.
-- it has backed and is not deserting Zaire's ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko.
Without the blessing of Rwanda and the rebels, a force might quickly be fighting instead of helping.
Without France, there is no obvious leader for the force.
This partly explains why the focus has shifted to a potentially huge civilian relief operation, transporting food and medicine westwards from Rwanda into eastern Zaire.
The plan is workable so long as the rebels in control of the area want it to be, but has little chance of reaching those refugees who have fled westwards deeper into Zaire.

Analysts say the rebels have every interest in feeding the three-four million citizens of wider eastern Zaire, which they hope to "liberate," at the world's expense. They need support for their broader campaign to overthrow Mobutu.
The relief plan suits the Tutsi army leaderships in Rwanda and Burundi. They want friends in control of a stable eastern Zaire, making it a de facto buffer state along their western borders.
But do Rwanda, Burundi and the rebels really care about the fate of 1.2 million Hutu refugees from Rwanda and Burundi in eastern Zaire?
The great bulk are Rwandans who fled to Zaire after many of them committed 1994's genocide against minority Tutsis and pro-opposition Hutus.
Thousands of armed men among the refugees have spent two years attacking their homelands and are now fighting alongside Zaire's demoralised army against the rebels.

Most of the refugees have scattered from their camps and are at the greatest risk of death from starvation and disease. But to reach them, aid workers will need safe passage from the rebels. Delays will cost thousands more lives.
Rwanda and the rebels have agreed to allow "corridors" for the refugees -- but only if they are one-way alleys back to Rwanda and Burundi.

For two years all but a trickle of refugees have refused to go home. They say they fear reprisals for the genocide or life as a guilt-ridden underclass below the Tutsi minority. They can point to the 80,000 Hutu genocide suspects already in Rwandan prisons without trial.

Faced with a miserable death in Zaire, the refugees might decide to give up the fight and go home. But the Hutu fighters among them will oppose any mass movement, fearing their own isolation in hostile territory.
And neither of the intervention plans, military or civilian, has explained how the ordinary Hutus will be separated from the armed element.
